title: DesiCrew
description: DesiCrew: Repositioned & branded a 19 year old business operations company to what it has become, a deployed intelligence AI enterprise.
subtitle: Build DesiCrew's brand, positioning, content engine, and outbound infrastructure so the quality of work happening inside the company becomes visible outside it.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: DesiCrew is a data and operations company with 19+ years of experience, delivering for some of the largest organisations in the world — the menus behind half of India's food orders, LIDAR for autonomous vehicles. The problem was never the work — it was the perception. DesiCrew was positioned as a rural BPO, not the company quietly building the data behind frontier AI. The company's growth had been built on relationships, referrals, and the quality of work speaking for itself.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text:
DesiCrew works on both sides of AI. It helps build AI — collecting and labelling the data that trains the models — and it runs on AI, handling enterprise operations faster and cleaner than most. The annotation companies can't run the operations. The big BPM players don't have the technical depth. DesiCrew has both, plus nineteen years a newer company can't fake.

So we stopped calling it a BPO and started calling it what it is: an AI operations company. Then we built everything around that — the positioning and messaging, one website instead of scattered ones, a new sales story, a content engine the leaders run themselves, and outbound that targets the right people instead of everyone.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: DesiCrew went from a set of six verticals, read as a legacy BPO, to a single brand with clear positioning and a complete rebrand. It is now positioned on both sides of AI. The leaders now publish in their own voice, the narrative finally matches the work, and the company the market sees is finally the one that's actually there.

cardHeadline: A 19-year-old company had become something its old category could no longer explain.
cardLine: We helped rebuild its positioning and narrative around the company it had actually become.

title: Luma Wars
description: Luma Wars: Built a game that fights review-bombing by never fighting back.
subtitle: Built a game that fights review-bombing by never fighting back.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: EDT is a D2C air fryer brand, built mostly around people setting up their first kitchen. Then the bots showed up, dropping fake one-star reviews in bulk. The question we kept asking ourselves was: "this is a real problem every D2C brand faces, what can we do different?" The usual answer is to report them and wait. We wanted to do something more real and impactful.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: The obvious was to write a post about it, but we decided to build a game. The brand stands up for itself without putting anyone down, and shooting back would have said the opposite. So we flipped it. You don't shoot the bots, you dodge them. Luma, the EDT air fryer, became the hero, wrapped in a Star Wars opening and an 8-bit look the audience grew up on. The score ran on founder and VC in-jokes, because founders were the ones playing. Mobile only, because that's where it would spread.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: 100k views and over a thousand people played. But the real result was the reaction. People watched a brand think this hard about a one-star review and turn it into something its own community wanted to pass around.

cardHeadline: Review bots were hitting a D2C brand. Reporting them and waiting wasn't much of an answer.
cardLine: So we built a game where you dodge the bots instead of shooting back — a brand standing up for itself without putting anyone down.

title: Pause
description: Pause: Built a mental health brand people actually loved by doing what no one else would — making them laugh.
subtitle: Built a mental health brand people actually loved by doing what no one else would — making them laugh.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: Mental health came with stigma, and the last thing people wanted was another earnest, overly-precious meditation app. Meanwhile the category was drowning in the same visual clichés — pastels, nature, soft whispers, and gentle hands resting on knees.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: Dark humour is how a lot of people actually deal with hard feelings. Instead of the expected "it's okay to not be okay" approach, we built Pause's brand voice around self-deprecating humour, honest emotional admission, and a tone that felt like talking to your sharpest friend — the one who makes you laugh about the thing you've been avoiding.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: When an entire category competes on sincerity, the funniest voice in the room wins. Pause launched with a 70+ NPS and a brand that didn't feel like a brand — it felt like a group chat. Users didn't just use the app, they shared it — because the content was worth sharing independent of the product.

cardHeadline: An entire category was competing on sincerity.
cardLine: We built a mental health brand around dark humour instead — the voice people actually use for hard feelings.

title: QAonCloud
description: QAonCloud: Repositioned, rebranded, and rebuilt a 12-year-old QA company from the ground up.
subtitle: Repositioned, rebranded, and rebuilt a 12-year-old QA company from the ground up.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: QAonCloud is a software testing company with 12+ years of experience and 60+ global clients. The problem wasn't the work — it was the brand. The existing website looked like every other generic IT services company: clip art icons, vague promises, and zero differentiation. In a market where every QA company says the same thing, QAonCloud had no reason for anyone to pick them over the next search result.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: We stripped everything back and found the one thing that was actually true and defensible: QAonCloud's AI-accelerated process genuinely delivered QA 40% faster than in-house teams. That became the entire brand. We repositioned from a generic "QA testing services company" to a specific, measurable promise — "40% faster QA. Accelerated by AI, driven by experts." Then we rebuilt the visual identity, rewrote every word on the site, and designed and developed a completely new web presence from scratch.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: The new site went from a generic enterprise template to a sharp, conversion-focused experience with clear positioning, real social proof, and a specific promise that no competitor was making. We also built a content strategy and outreach programme to drive inbound and outbound leads.

cardHeadline: A better product truth was hiding inside a generic services story.
cardLine: We found the sharper promise in the business and rebuilt its market expression around it.

title: Origin One
description: Origin One: Increased sales by 153% in 4 weeks via user research, media buying & advertising.
subtitle: Increased sales by 153% in 4 weeks via user research, media buying & advertising.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: Origin One is a premium stationery brand with a product people loved once they tried it — but almost no one was trying it. Advertising existed but it was scattered and directionless. There was no clear positioning, no consistent creative, and no strategy behind what was being spent. The brand had strong social proof from existing customers but had never used it.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: Stationery isn't a rational purchase — nobody needs another notebook. It's an emotional one. We built a creative strategy around what the product actually made people feel: the texture of the paper, the ritual of writing, the quiet satisfaction of something beautifully made. We paired visceral, sensory-driven ads with real customer stories that had been sitting unused. Then we built the media buying infrastructure to put it all in front of the right people.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: Sales increased by 153% in 4 weeks. What started as an advertising engagement has since expanded into full CRO — optimising the funnel, improving the user experience, and turning one-time buyers into repeat customers.

cardLine: Customer understanding, creative and distribution came together to move a clearer commercial proposition into the market.

title: QwikBuild
description: QwikBuild: The market changed. We rebuilt the positioning, value proposition and website to change with it.
subtitle: The market changed. We rebuilt QwikBuild's positioning, value proposition and website to change with it.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text:
QwikBuild began in a category moving at absurd speed.

Products changed. Competitors changed. What users expected from AI software changed. Language that felt new six months earlier could become generic almost overnight.

At some point the problem stopped being how do we market the existing proposition better, and became: what should QwikBuild mean now?

sections.label: THE EVIDENCE
sections.text:
Our earlier work with QwikBuild had given us something more useful than opinions.

We had real signal from positioning, advertising, channels, customer response and product adoption. We could see what people understood, what created interest, what created confusion, and how the competitive context around the product was changing. That signal had already informed a pivot on the product itself.

The market had moved enough that simply improving the old story would have been the wrong answer.

sections.label: THE REPOSITIONING
sections.text:
So we went back to the product, the company, the audience and the competitive landscape.

We rebuilt the positioning and value proposition around the reality QwikBuild was operating in now. Then we translated that into a new website and a clearer market expression.

The aim was not cosmetic change. It was to make the company easier to understand for the market it actually wanted to win.

sections.label: THE PATTERN
sections.text:
QwikBuild is a useful example of the kind of problem we want to get very good at.

A company changes. The market changes. The old explanation stops being useful.

So you go back to what is true now — and build the new meaning from there.

cardHeadline: The AI market changed. QwikBuild needed to change with it.
cardLine: We rebuilt the positioning, value proposition and website around the market QwikBuild was actually competing in.

title: Attis Insider
description: Attis Insider: Launched India's first biohacking community with a viral campaign and a bag of magic beans.
subtitle: Launched India's first biohacking community with a viral campaign and a bag of magic beans.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: India's biohacking space was nonexistent. There were no dedicated brands, no communities, no cultural conversation around the idea that optimisation wasn't just for athletes or tech bros. Attis wanted to build a community before selling a product — but "biohacking" sounded intimidating.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: We created Attis Insider — a membership-style community that made biohacking feel like a culture, not a science experiment. The launch campaign, "Magic Pills", was deliberately provocative: we sent mystery packages branded as pills to health influencers and content creators with no context.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: The campaign generated over 100k organic views, 500+ social mentions, and 1000+ community signups — all on ₹0 ad spend. The mystery packaging created FOMO-driven sharing loops that outperformed paid campaigns.

cardHeadline: India had no biohacking culture, so there was nothing to belong to yet.
cardLine: We launched the community before the product, with a deliberately provocative campaign and no media spend.

title: Attis Campaigns
description: Attis Campaigns: Two viral campaigns that exposed nerves. Zero ad spend. Massive reach.
subtitle: Two viral campaigns that exposed nerves. Zero ad spend. Massive reach.

sections.label: THE LANDSCAPE
sections.text: After building the community, Attis needed to convert attention into revenue. But typical health-brand advertising — clean product shots, benefit-focused copy, influencer unboxings — would have killed the edge that made the brand interesting.

sections.label: THE INSIGHT
sections.text: We ran two campaigns designed to expose nerves. Each one made people uncomfortable enough to stop scrolling, curious enough to click, and convinced enough to buy. The campaigns leaned into Attis's counter-cultural positioning rather than softening it for conversion.

sections.label: THE OUTCOME
sections.text: Two viral campaigns. 850+ product orders. 250k+ organic views. The brand maintained its edge while proving that provocative creative isn't just for awareness — it converts.

cardHeadline: The community had attention. It hadn't become revenue.
cardLine: Two campaigns that converted by keeping the brand's edge rather than softening it.
